title: What the Lord requires (Micah 6:8)
hook: to do judgment, to love mercy, and to walk solicitous with thy God

segments.voice: Yesterday, justice like a torrent: Amos the herdsman at the royal shrine. Your line was justice that runs all year.

Micah, called the Morasthite after his hometown, preached in the days of the same kings as Isaiah, and in chapter six he stages a trial. God takes his people to court, with the mountains and the foundations of the earth as the jury. Then God speaks first, and it isn't an accusation. It's a question: my people, what have I done to thee? How have I been a burden to you? Answer me. On Good Friday that line is the heart of the Reproaches, chanted while the cross is venerated: in Latin, popule meus, quid feci tibi.
screen: `THE MOUNTAINS AS THE JURY.` → `MY PEOPLE, WHAT HAVE I DONE TO THEE?` → `HEARD AGAIN ON GOOD FRIDAY.`

segments.voice: The people answer, and you can feel them getting nervous. What should I bring? Burnt offerings? Calves a year old? Thousands of rams, many thousands of fat goats, or, as the Hebrew has it, rivers of oil? Should I give my firstborn for my sin? Each offer is bigger than the last, until it becomes unthinkable. Then the prophet cuts through it, in the Douay-Rheims: "I will shew thee, O man, what is good, and what the Lord requireth of thee: Verily, to do judgment, and to love mercy, and to walk solicitous with thy God." O man: in Hebrew, adam, any human being, not just one nation. And three things, none of them expensive. Do judgment: act justly, Amos's word yesterday. Love mercy: the Hebrew is chesed, the steady loyal love met in Ruth; not just merciful acts now and then, but loving it. The third is the strangest. The Hebrew is hatznea lechet, and the first word is unusual and hard to pin down; translators reach for modestly, carefully, attentively. The Latin made it solicitous, so the Douay says walk solicitous: careful, the way you walk beside someone you don't want to lose. The King James says walk humbly, the way the line is often quoted. Both are trying to catch one hard word. Notice the verb, too: walk. Not arrive. A walk is daily, one step after another, and it's done with someone. The people offered rivers of oil. God asked for a way of walking.
screen: `THOUSANDS OF RAMS, RIVERS OF OIL?` · `O MAN: ADAM, ANY HUMAN BEING.` · `JUSTICE, CHESED, AND A CAREFUL WALK.` · `SOLICITOUS OR HUMBLY: ONE HARD WORD.` · then, large: `WHAT THE LORD REQUIRETH OF THEE.`

segments.voice: Say the three over slowly, do justly, love mercy, walk humbly, and notice which one tugs at you: something unfair to set right, someone to be kind to steadily, or a walk that's been a little too loud and sure. Pick just one, and picture the moment you'll live it. If you pray, offer that one step to God.
hatznea lechet. Hebrew for walking carefully with God: Micah's third requirement, after doing justice and loving mercy. Today's word.
Your line: walk humbly. Justly, mercifully, and carefully, with God beside you. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: On Good Friday the Church chants the Reproaches, built on Micah 6:3, during the veneration of the cross, and Micah 6:8 is quoted in Catholic teaching on justice and mercy.

fork.setup: you're in God's courtroom with the mountains as jury. you want to make things right. what do you offer?
options: thousands of rams and ten thousand rivers of oil.

fork.reveal: Micah cuts through the bidding war: I will shew thee, O man, what is good. three things, none of them expensive.

original.note: Hebrew: to walk modestly or carefully. the first word is unusual; the Latin has solicitous, the King James humbly.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice verse for a poster.
what it means: the answer to a people trying to buy God's favor: not rivers of oil, but justice, loyal love, and a careful daily walk.
what a scholar hears: adam, any human; chesed, loyal love; and hatznea, an unusual word, translated solicitous in the Latin and humbly in English.
guess: walking in a long procession to the Temple
bringing rivers of oil as an offering

chat.says: What does Micah say God really wants instead of big offerings?
options: To do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly, carefully, with God.
Bigger sacrifices, even rivers of oil, to show you're truly sorry.
To keep the law perfectly, so there's nothing left to forgive.
chat.meaning: The people offered more and more. Micah cuts through: what the Lord requires is justice, loving mercy, and a careful walk with God.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): Micah now introduced from 1:1 (the Morasthite, same kings as Isaiah) instead of an unsourced 'village near the border'; 6:7 paraphrase now follows the Douay ('fat goats') and flags 'rivers of oil' as the Hebrew; cut the 'almost nowhere else' rarity claim and 'most English speakers'; fork reveal now echoes the Douay ('I will shew thee'), not the KJV ('he hath shewed thee'); replaced KJV 'wearied' with a plain paraphrase.
Douay-Rheims wording of Micheas 6:8 checked against the outline's own hook ('to do judgment, to love mercy, and to walk solicitous with thy God'); the opening clause is from memory. Please confirm.
The fork reveal paraphrases 'he hath shewed thee' (KJV-style); it is not marked as a quotation.
Hatznea (tsana') appears elsewhere only at Proverbs 11:2 (as tsanua). Confirm 'almost nowhere else'.
Micah of Moresheth, contemporary with Isaiah (8th century BC): confirm 'a village near the border'.
The Reproaches (Improperia) and 'Popule meus, quid feci tibi?' from Micah 6:3: confirm their place in the current Good Friday rite (sung during the adoration of the cross).
Restyled 2026-10-07 (job 2): voice tightened; content and sources unchanged.
